\chapter{Joining Things Together}
\label{ch:ml-cherkkuka}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two or more nouns in one list, and offer somebody a choice between two, using the ending Malayalam puts on each item rather than a word between them.}

From cold: water and rice, tea or coffee, and a three-item list carrying three endings.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[veḷḷavuṁ ariyuṁ]{\ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും} — where Malayalam puts its \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C70-um}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for water. Say the word for rice, the raw grain.

Now try to say the two of them together, as one list. \textbf{You have had both words since chapter fifteen and no way to put them side by side.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{Malayalam's \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} is not a word that stands between two things. It is a syllable that goes on the end of each of them.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും}} — \emph{veḷḷavuṁ ariyuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}water and rice\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The piece doing the work is \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}} (\emph{-uṁ}), and it appears \textbf{twice} — once on \emph{water}, once on \emph{rice}. English hangs one \emph{and} in the gap between two nouns; Malayalam hangs one \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}} off the back of every noun in the list and leaves the gap empty.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Malayalam} \\
\midrule
water \textbf{and} rice & water\textbf{-uṁ} rice\textbf{-uṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Count the joins, not the gaps.} Two items means two \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}}, and a list with only one of them on it is a list that is still waiting for something.

\begin{cousinweb}
The ending changes the word slightly as it lands, and the two changes here are the two you will meet most:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}} ends in \textbf{-\ml{ം}}. That \textbf{-\ml{ം}} becomes \textbf{-\ml{വും}}: \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളവും}}.
  \item \textbf{\ml{അരി}} ends in a vowel. A \textbf{\ml{യ്}} slides in to keep the two vowels apart: \textbf{\ml{അരിയും}}.
\end{itemize}

Neither is a special case to memorise. Both are the same instinct a mouth has when one sound runs into another, and Malayalam writes down what the mouth already does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും}
  \item how many times the joining piece appears in that list
  \item what sits in the gap between the two words (nothing)
  \item which of the two words changed its last letter, and to what
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does Malayalam put its \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} — between the items or on them? (On them.) How many \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}} does a two-item list carry? (Two.) What is in the space between the two words? (Nothing at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veḷḷavuṁ ariyuṁ pāluṁ]{\ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും} \ml{പാലും} — every item, however many there are}

\label{lesson:ML-C70-um-more}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{water and rice}. Count the joining endings in it.

Now say the word for milk on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും} \ml{പാലും}} — \emph{veḷḷavuṁ ariyuṁ pāluṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}water, rice and milk\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Three items, three endings.} English changes shape as a list grows — it drops commas in and saves its single \emph{and} for the last pair. Malayalam changes nothing: every item carries the ending, and a list of five would carry five.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Malayalam} \\
\midrule
water, rice \textbf{and} milk & water\textbf{-uṁ} rice\textbf{-uṁ} milk\textbf{-uṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is a rule you can extend without being taught the extension, which is worth noticing because English lists are one of the fiddlier things a learner of English has to absorb.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} gives the third landing, and it completes the set you need:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a noun ending in \textbf{-\ml{ം}} $\to$ \textbf{-\ml{വും}}: \ml{വെള്ളം}, \ml{വെള്ളവും}
  \item a noun ending in a \textbf{vowel} $\to$ a letter slides in, chosen by that vowel; after \textbf{\ml{ഇ}} it is \textbf{\ml{യ്}}: \ml{അരി}, \ml{അരിയും}
  \item a noun ending in \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} $\to$ the letter unfurls to \textbf{\ml{ല}} and takes the ending plainly: \ml{പാൽ}, \ml{പാലും}
\end{itemize}

That last one looks like a change and is not. \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} is the compressed, end-of-word form of \textbf{\ml{ല}}; putting anything after it gives the full letter back, because it is no longer at the end.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും} \ml{പാലും}
  \item how many endings a list of five items would carry
  \item what English does to a list that Malayalam does not
  \item why \ml{പാൽ} ends up as \ml{പാലും} rather than \ml{പാൽും}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the ending go on every item or only the last? (Every one.) What happens to \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} when something follows it? (It unfurls back to \textbf{\ml{ല}}.) How many endings in a four-item list? (Four.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cāyayō kāppiyō]{\ml{ചായയോ} \ml{കാപ്പിയോ} — the same trick, a different answer}

\label{lesson:ML-C70-o}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for tea. Say the word for coffee.

Now try to offer somebody the pair of them — not both, one or the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ചായയോ} \ml{കാപ്പിയോ}?} — \emph{cāyayō kāppiyō?} — \textquotedblleft{}tea or coffee?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{-\ml{ഓ}} (\emph{-ō}) is the ending for a choice, and it works exactly the way the joining ending does: \textbf{one on each item, nothing in the gap.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{what a list of two means} \\
\midrule
-\ml{ഉം} ... -\ml{ഉം} & both of them \\
-\ml{ഓ} ... -\ml{ഓ} & one of them \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The construction is identical and only the vowel changes.} Having learned where Malayalam puts a joining ending, you already know where it puts a choosing one — which is the reason these two belong in one chapter rather than fifty pages apart.

The \textbf{\ml{യ്}} glide appears again on both words here, for the same reason it appeared on \textbf{\ml{അരി}}: both end in a vowel, and two vowels meeting want something between them.

\begin{cousinweb}
There is also a separate word, \textbf{\ml{അല്ലെങ്കിൽ}} (\emph{alleṅkil}), which stands between two options the way English \emph{or} does:

\begin{quote}
\ml{ചായ} \textbf{\ml{അല്ലെങ്കിൽ}} \ml{കാപ്പി}
\end{quote}

Both are heard. The ending is the shorter and more usual thing in a spoken question; the standing word is easier to reach for while the ending is still new, and it is the one that will look familiar on a page because it sits where an English reader expects \emph{or} to sit.

\textbf{Reach for whichever arrives first.} A learner who says the long one has said the thing; the ending will come with hearing it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{ചായയോ} \ml{കാപ്പിയോ}
  \item the same offer using the standing word instead
  \item what \ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} would mean instead
  \item which single letter is the whole difference between the two
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending offers a choice? (\textbf{-\ml{ഓ}}.) Which one means you get both? (\textbf{-\ml{ഉം}}.) Where do they go — between the items or on them? (On them, one each.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cērkkuka]{\ml{ചേർക്കുക} — two endings, from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R70-cherkkuka}



\begin{quote}
Close the three lessons before this one. Say the word for water and the word for tea, with nothing in front of you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you want} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
both & \ml{വെള്ളവും} \ml{അരിയും} \\
one of them & \ml{ചായയോ} \ml{കാപ്പിയോ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{One habit covers both}: the ending goes on every item and the gap stays empty. Change the vowel and you change the question from \emph{both} to \emph{which}.

That is the whole of this chapter, and it is worth saying how late it arrives. \textbf{Sixty-nine chapters of this book gave you words and no way to put two of them side by side} — five body parts, five animals, five kitchen words, and until now no way to ask for two of them at once.

\begin{cousinweb}
The ending lands three ways, and all three are the mouth rather than a rule:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{-\ml{ം}} becomes \textbf{-\ml{വും}} — \ml{വെള്ളം}, \ml{വെള്ളവും}
  \item a \textbf{vowel} takes a \textbf{\ml{യ്}} first — \ml{അരി}, \ml{അരിയും} · \ml{ചായ}, \ml{ചായയോ}
  \item \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} unfurls to \textbf{\ml{ല}} — \ml{പാൽ}, \ml{പാലും}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item water and rice, from memory
  \item tea or coffee, from memory
  \item water, rice and milk — three items, three endings
  \item which vowel turns a list into a choice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a joining ending go? (On every item.) What sits between the items? (Nothing.) Which ending asks somebody to pick one? (\textbf{-\ml{ഓ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
